nameStory: The Bay Polypore gets its name from its rich reddish-brown cap color that resembles the warm, earthy tones of bay leaves or a bay horse's coat. However, it's also called the black-footed polypore because of its distinctively dark stem base, which often turns completely black as the fungus matures.
description: Bay Polypore is a substantial bracket fungus that grows from dead or dying hardwood and conifer trees. It features a distinctive dark brown to reddish-brown cap that can reach an impressive 10 inches across, supported by a thick stem that's notably darker at the bottom. Unlike many bracket fungi that grow directly from tree trunks, this species has a proper stem and often grows from the ground near decaying wood.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: The stem is the star feature - often completely black at the base, sometimes brown at the top. It feels firm and woody, with a distinctly darker coloration toward the bottom that's unmistakable once you see it.

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Rich dark brown to reddish-brown coloring, like dark chocolate or coffee grounds. The surface feels smooth to slightly velvety when fresh, and can grow quite large - up to 10 inches across.

idTips.label: Pores
idTips.description: Tiny white to cream-colored pores on the underside instead of gills. The pore surface may bruise slightly yellow when pressed firmly with your finger.

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Fresh specimens have a mild, earthy mushroom smell - nothing unpleasant or strongly distinctive that would help with identification.

habitat: Look for Bay Polypore in mixed and deciduous forests throughout New England, especially where there are dying or recently dead hardwood trees like oak, maple, and birch. It often appears to be growing from the ground but is actually connected to buried wood or root systems. You'll find it in both lowland and upland forests, particularly in areas with good moisture retention.

seasonality.spring: New growth begins as soil warms and spring rains provide moisture. Young specimens will show the freshest coloring and firmest texture.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when most specimens reach full size. Fresh caps will show the richest brown coloring during humid summer months.
seasonality.fall: Still actively growing and easiest to spot as leaves drop. The contrast between the dark stems and fallen leaves makes identification easier.
seasonality.winter: Older specimens persist and become tougher and more weathered. The distinctive black stem base remains visible even when caps fade or decay.

funFact: Despite its common name suggesting it grows near water, Bay Polypore creates a "white rot" that actually helps forest ecosystems by breaking down lignin - the tough compound that gives wood its strength - essentially performing nature's recycling by turning dead trees back into soil nutrients.
confusionNotes: The black stem base is your best friend for identification - no other common polypore in New England has such a distinctively dark stem bottom. If you're unsure, just look down at where the stem meets the ground.
contextualKnowledge: This species was recently moved from the genus Royoporus to Picipes, so you might see it listed under its old scientific name Royoporus badius in older field guides. The name changes don't affect identification, but it's good to know when comparing different sources.
compareHints: Bay Polypore's black stem base immediately separates it from its relatives in the Picipes genus. While Picipes melanopus also has a dark stem, Bay Polypore's is consistently blacker at the base and the cap color is more distinctly reddish-brown rather than grayish-brown.
